newsitem.title: MEXICO: All-powerful Mexican union boss dies at 97.
newsitem.headline: All-powerful Mexican union boss dies at 97.

text.p: Fidel Velazquez, an all-powerful union boss whose unswerving support for nine presidents made him a living symbol of Mexico's monolithic political system, died on Saturday in office at age 97.

One of the country's last major figures to have lived through the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, Velazquez's extraordinary career took him from milkman to powerbroker between labour and government for more than half a century.

Progressively going deaf and blind, losing the use of one arm and needing help to walk, the cigar-chomping Velazquez refused to contemplate resigning as president of the Confederation of Mexican Workers (CTM) until the end despite increasingly embarrassing public appearances.

But such was Velazquez's influence that, despite his falling asleep occasionally during meetings, even President Ernesto Zedillo felt obliged to lead a three-minute standing ovation for the union boss at a CTM event last year.

The ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has ruled Mexico with an iron grip since the 1920s, relying for its political domination on alliances of convenience with business, labour and the military.
Velazquez was the pillar which constituted the support of organised labour for the PRI during more than a half century -- a reign during which he outlived three biographers.

"In many ways, in fact, it was the regime's success in controlling labour after the Revolution that created the foundations for the entire system," wrote journalist Alan Riding in his 1984 book on Mexico, "Distant Neighbours."
"But the strength of this arrangement ... leaned heavily on one man, Fidel Velazquez," he wrote.

Born on April 24, 1900, into a peasant family in the village of San Pedro Azcapotzaltongo in the state of Mexico, Velazquez spent his early years rising at dawn to sow fields before school. His education finished at the age of 14.
After a brief spell in a sawmill, Velazquez showed his political mettle at the age of 21 when he was fired from his milkman's job for organising Mexico's first milk union.
The union quickly recruited more than 8,000 members and affiliated itself to the Mexican Regional Workers Confederation (CROM), then the most powerful union federation.
But in 1928 the union withdrew during a power struggle and Velazquez helped found a rival organisation which finally evolved in 1936 into the dominant CTM.

First elected head of the CTM in 1941 while the Second World War was raging, Velazquez clung tenaciously to his post until he died, fighting off challengers successfully, apart from a brief period from 1947-50 when he temporarily lost control.
President after president took pains to win his support and that of his federation, which represented more than 11,000 unions and some 6 million workers.
Former President Jose Lopez Portillo described Velazquez's impact on generations of Mexicans by saying: "The history of Mexico cannot be understood without Fidel Velazquez."
A lifelong anti-Communist, Velazquez was remarkably pragmatic, a trait that allowed him to co-exist with populist leaders as well as the free marketeers of the 1980s and 1990s.

The CTM's house newspaper gave a revealing insight into his character in a eulogistic 95th birthday tribute in which it asked the secrets of Velazquez's lifelong success and ventured as one of the answers:
"Perhaps because he has managed to understand like no one else the rules of the system."

Velazquez sided with the Mexican government in 1958 when it crushed a railroad workers' strike and was silent a decade later when Mexican soldiers gunned down students in the capital during a protest.
Criticised for excessive cosiness with the government, he claimed the close relationship yielded more gains for workers.
Velazquez's most famous phrase: "He who moves won't come out in the photo," summed up his philosophy of sticking loyally to the government and not rocking the boat.
The influence of "Don Fidel," as he was reverently called, began to wane during the 1980s as years of declining real wages undermined worker loyalty to the CTM.

Detractors questioned his use of lavish motorcades to move around the city and accused him of being out of touch with ordinary workers, whose spending power has shrunk by two-thirds over the past 16 years.

In one memorable moment in 1995 during the economic turmoil following a shock devaluation of the peso, Velazquez was denounced after calling on workers to donate a day's salary to the government to help it out.
He leaves a wife, Nora Quintana, and three children.
